The wind and cloud vocabulary at v.4-5, שֹׁמֵ֥ר ר֖וּחַ (oshb:Eccl.11.4, tier: byte) and מַה דֶּ֣רֶךְ הָר֔וּחַ (oshb:Eccl.11.5, tier: byte), is literal weather observation, not the idiomatic chasing-wind or wind-thought refrain found elsewhere in the book (the bare ruach word-bound form occurs at 20 verses book-wide, and these two ch-11 sites carry it in its plain, non-idiomatic sense); it stays texture, not a boundary device.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: A single admonition-sentence closes the chapter. Its actual opening words are גַּ֣ם בְּמַדָּֽעֲךָ֗ (oshb:Eccl.10.20, tier: byte) — "even in your thought" — with the curse clauses following, spliced as מֶ֚לֶךְ אַל תְּקַלֵּ֔ל (oshb:Eccl.10.20, tier: byte) — "the king, do not curse" — matching “Don’t curse the king” (web:Eccl.10.20). Near its close stands an inline ketiv/qere pair, הכנפים כְּנָפַ֖יִם (oshb:Eccl.10.20, ketiv/qere; tier: byte), on the word for "wings," matching “that which has wings may tell the matter” (web:Eccl.10.20). The verse carries a doubled negated prefix-conjugation (jussive-pattern) form used for negative commands, not a true imperative ("do not curse the king...do not curse the rich"); it is one grammatical sentence and is held as a single_saying under the sentence-zone default, closing the chapter.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Classifying this verse as an admonition_unit rather than single_saying is rejected because the whole warning is confined to one grammatical sentence rather than a multi-verse counsel block.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The bridge opens in third-person reflection, “Truly the light is sweet” (web:Eccl.11.7), turning at v.8 to a conditional: כִּ֣י אִם שָׁנִ֥ים הַרְבֵּ֛ה יִחְיֶ֥ה הָאָדָ֖ם (oshb:Eccl.11.8, tier: byte) — "if a man lives many years" — followed by its own apodosis, בְּכֻלָּ֣ם יִשְׂמָ֑ח (oshb:Eccl.11.8, tier: byte) — “let him rejoice in them all” (web:Eccl.11.8), and its own remember-clause, וְיִזְכֹּר֙ (oshb:Eccl.11.8, tier: byte) — "and let him remember" — matching “let him remember the days of darkness” (web:Eccl.11.8). At v.9 the register shifts to direct second-person vocative address, spliced as שְׂמַ֧ח בָּח֣וּר (oshb:Eccl.11.9, tier: byte) — "rejoice, young man" — matching “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (web:Eccl.11.9). Both halves are held as one row because the rejoice root recurs at v.8 and v.9 (though the remember root stands at 1 of 4 verses in the span, v.8, not repeated at v.9-10), continuing without a discourse-frame break; the 3rd-to-2nd-person shift at v.8/9 is disclosed as a live alternative seam. An unbroken 2ms-imperative chain — שְׂמַ֧ח (oshb:Eccl.11.9) here, וְהָסֵ֥ר (oshb:Eccl.11.10) in the verse that follows, and וּזְכֹר֙ (oshb:Eccl.12.1) in the unit after that — together with the near-identical youth-phrase catchword (בִּימֵ֣י בְחוּרוֹתֶ֔ךָ (oshb:Eccl.11.9) against בִּימֵ֖י בְּחוּרֹתֶ֑יךָ (oshb:Eccl.12.1), sweep: 2 verses) both cross this unit's own closing seam into the poem that follows; the row still closes at v.10 because the register there completes the youth-address begun at v.9, while the imperative chain's continuation into the poem is disclosed as cross-seam texture rather than adopted as a boundary shift. The unit closes on “youth and the dawn of life are vanity” (web:Eccl.11.10), immediately before the aging-allegory poem's own imperative opens.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting v.7-8 (third-person reflection) from v.9-10 (direct youth address) at the person-register shift is a live alternative, disclosed rather than adopted, because the rejoice root continues across the shift without an intervening discourse frame.
